actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This species was previously known only from northern (Boulenger 1903, Orlov 1997, Inger et al. 1999, Orlov et al. 2002, Nguyen et al. 2009) and central (Luu et al. 2014) Viet Nam between 470–1,500 m asl. Following revision of the genus in China (Hou et al. 2017), Theloderma kwangsiense has now been synonymised with this species. The distribution of the species now extends through the south of China including the island of Hainan, southwards through northern and central Viet Nam and across the border in to central eastern Lao People's Democratic Republic (Lao PDR) (Hou et al. 2017, Brakels et al. 2021). In China it has been recorded from Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan provinces, and is expected to occur more widely in these provinces, as well as the neighbouring provinces of Fujian, Hunan, Yunnan and Zhejiang, where there is suitable habitat near know localities (Hou et al. 2017). It has been recorded between 500–1,320 m asl.
documentation.population: This species is known from several studies (Boulenger 1903, Orlov 1997, Inger et al. 1999, Luu et al. 2014, etc.), and was described as abundant at Tam Dao, northern Viet Nam in the 1990s (Orlov 1997). Hou et al. (2017) described it as rare as it can be difficult to find, although this may be because it spends most of its time in tree holes making it difficult to detect. Deforestation continues to affect habitat in this species' range (Sodhi et al. 2009), and is very likely causing some declines.
documentation.habitats: This species occurs in primary subtropical and tropical forest and is sometimes associated with steep, rocky cliffs in Viet Nam (Orlov 1997). It is usually found sheltering in water-filled tree holes or in wet moss (Hou et al. 2017). Reproduction has been observed between March and December (Orlov et al. 2006). This species deposits eggs in water-filled rock cavities, where the tadpoles remain until metamorphosis (Orlov 1997).
documentation.threats: Habitat loss and degradation due to the effects of rapidly expanding agriculture is an ongoing threat to biodiversity throughout southeast Asia (Sodhi et al. 2009). Satellite imagery reveals areas of land cleared for agriculture throughout much of this species' range, however its occurrence in steep, rocky areas (Orlov 1997) may offer some protection from habitat loss associated with agriculture. Despite this species having been successfully bred in captivity (Orlov et al. 2006, Gawor et al. 2012), it may also be threatened by collection from the wild to meet the demand for the international pet trade, as is the case for similarly attractive frog species from the region (Rowley et al. 2010). In China, its habitat is threatened by agriculture, logging, construction of dams for hydropower, as well as, illegal collection for the pet trade.
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions In-Place
This species is known from a number of protected areas including Tam Dao (Orlov et al. 1997, Inger et al. 1999) and Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Parks (Luu et al. 2014) in Viet Nam, and Nakai Nam Theun National Park in Lao PDR (Brakels et al. 2021), as well as, Shiwandashan National Nature Reserve in China. There are captive populations of the species in Vietnamese (Gawore et al. 2012) and European (Orlov et al. 2006, Rauhaus et al. 2012) zoological institutions, as well as in private collections.

Research Needed
Further research on its distribution, threats, the size and trends of its population, and rates of harvest would inform conservation decisions.
documentation.use_trade: This species is in the international pet trade and is in relatively high demand due to its attractive form and colouration; an online search in December 2015 revealed a number of websites selling this species for approximately US $60–120 per individual (T. Cutajar pers. comm. 2015). The species is also kept in a number of zoos (Rauhaus et al. 2012).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern as this species is widespread and its population is unlikely to be declining fast enough for listing in a more threatened category.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Theloderma kwangsiensis has been synonymised with T. corticale by Hou et al. (2017).
